title: An-Nisa
label: Plain-English commentary
intro:
An-Nisa, "The Women," is a Medinan surah of 176 verses. It was revealed in Al-Madinah: Al-ʿAwfi reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said so, and Ibn Marduwyah recorded similar statements from ʿAbdullāh bin Az-Zubayr and Zayd bin Thābit. It takes its name from the many rulings it contains concerning women, marriage, inheritance and the family, but its reach is wider than its name: it moves from the creation of humanity and the bonds of kinship through the laws of property, marriage and inheritance, to the conduct of believers and hypocrites, fighting in Allah's cause, and the final reckoning.

The surah opens with the command to be mindful of Allah, and it is the same note on which Sūrat Āl ʿImrān ended. There the exhortation to taqwā (being mindful of Allah) came as a closing reminder. Here it comes as an opening command. The previous surah had spoken of battles, of the treatment of opponents, and of misappropriation of spoils. This surah turns to the rights a person owes to those closest to him: orphans, relatives, wives. Some of these rights can be enforced by law, like buying and selling, lease and wages. Others, the rights of children, parents, husband and wife, and of relatives toward one another, depend on civilised behaviour, respect, love and care, and above all on a genuine desire to do good. Such things cannot be weighed or settled by agreement, so the only way to secure them is taqwā, the fear of Allah and of what comes in the life to come. Taqwā, on this view, is more effective than government and law together. Hence the surah begins: "O humanity! Be mindful of your Lord Who created you from a single soul, and from it He created its mate, and through both He spread countless men and women. And be mindful of Allah—in Whose Name you appeal to one another—and ˹honour˺ family ties. Surely Allah is ever Watchful over you."

The verse argues from creation to kinship. Allah created all human beings from one person, Ādam (Adam), and from him created his mate, Hawwāʾ (Eve), from his left rib, from his back while he slept. When Ādam woke and saw her he was drawn to her and she to him. From the two of them Allah spread many men and women across the world, in different shapes, colours and languages, and all of them return to Him. Because they share one origin, all human beings are brothers and sisters, and no distinction of race, caste, colour or language may be made the measure of worth. The same origin also tightens the bond within families, and the verse ends by warning against cutting family ties: the word translated "family ties" is al-arḥām, the plural of raḥm, "womb," and the bond it names is the bond of blood. To maintain it is ilāt ar-raḥm. To sever it is qaṭʿ ar-raḥm.

The verse also teaches why Allah should be feared: He is watchful over everyone, always. He sees every deed and every circumstance, including the intentions and motives of the heart. Doing things half-heartedly, or only for fear of embarrassment, is not accepted. This is why the Qur'an does not lay down laws in cold print like the laws of governments, but combines the law with the training of minds and hearts. The verse was also the one the Prophet ﷺ used to recite as part of his address when solemnising a marriage, so reciting it in the khutbah of nikah (the marriage sermon) is a perennial revival of the sunnah (the Prophet's practice). Its address, "O mankind," includes all human beings, men and women, those alive at the time and those to come until the Day of Judgment. "Lord" was chosen from among Allah's names because He is the One who nurtures and sustains, and the thought of rising against Him is terribly dangerous. The verse also says that people demand their rights from one another in Allah's name, so one who expects others to fear Allah must fear Him himself. The closing warning about family ties means that any shortcoming in caring for near relatives, whether on the father's side or the mother's, must be avoided.

Several hadiths develop the point. The Prophet ﷺ said, "Whoever likes to have his livelihood made plentiful and his age extended for him should maintain good relations with his near of kin." Another hadith, reported by ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām, says that when the Prophet ﷺ came to Madinah al-Tayyibah the first words he heard were: "O men, make a practice of greeting each other with salām, and feed people for the pleasure of Allah, and treat near relations well, and pray by night while people sleep, and you will enter Paradise in peace." Maymūnah, the Mother of the Faithful, freed a bondwoman and was told by the Prophet ﷺ that giving her to her maternal uncle would have brought a greater reward, and he said that charity to the needy is charity, while charity to a near relative is twofold: charity and kinship. He also warned: "A breaker of blood relationships shall not enter Paradise," and "Mercy shall not descend upon a people among whom there is a breaker of blood relationships." A further report says that Allah proclaimed, "I shall associate Myself with one who strengthens the ties of kinship and detach Myself from one who severs them." The Prophet ﷺ also recited this verse and "O you who believe! Have taqwā of Allah. And let every person look to what he has sent forth for the tomorrow" (59:18) to a delegation from Muḍar who had come wearing striped woollen clothes out of poverty, after the Zuhr prayer, and encouraged them to give sadaqah (charity), saying, "A man gave sadaqah from his dinar, from his dirham, from his ṣāʿ of wheat, from his ṣāʿ of dates." Muslim recorded this, and Aḥmad and the collectors of the sunan recorded it from Ibn Masʿūd. An authentic hadith says, "Woman was created from a rib. Verily, the most curved portion of the rib is its upper part, so, if you should try to straighten it, you will break it, but if you leave it as it is, it will remain crooked." Another authentic hadith says, "Worship Allah as if you see Him, for even though you cannot see Him, He sees you." The material also records that the mutual-rights phrase "through Whom you demand your mutual rights" refers, according to Ibrāhīm, Mujāhid and Al-Ḥasan, to people saying "I ask you by Allah, and then by the relation of the raḥim," while Ad-Dahhāk said it means fearing Allah when conducting transactions and contracts, and that the command to honour the womb means not cutting family ties but keeping and honouring them, as Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, Al-Ḥasan, Ad-Dahhāk, Ar-Rabīʿ and others stated. Allah's watchfulness is also echoed in "And Allah is Witness over all things" (58:6).

The surah's virtues are recorded too. Ibn Masʿūd said there are five verses in Sūrat An-Nisāʾ that he would prefer to the life of this world and all that is in it: "Surely, Allah wrongs not even the weight of an atom" (4:40). "If you avoid the great sins which you are forbidden to do" (4:31). "Verily, Allah forgives not that partners should be set up with Him, but He forgives except that to whom He wills" (4:48). "If they, when they had been unjust to themselves, had come to you" (4:64), and "And whoever does evil or wrongs himself, but afterwards seeks Allah's forgiveness, he will find Allah Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful" (4:110). Al-Ḥakīm recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said, "Ask me about Sūrat An-Nisāʾ, for I learned the Qur'an when I was still young," and said this hadith is ṣaḥīḥ according to the criteria of the two Ṣaḥīḥs, though they did not collect it. Al-Ḥakīm recorded the statement of Ibn Masʿūd in his Mustadrak.

As for what the surah covers, it begins with this foundation of taqwā and kinship, then sets out the rights of orphans and the protection of their property, the laws of marriage including polygamy and dowry, the management of the property of those not yet of age, and the Islamic law of inheritance, including the shares of parents, spouses, children and siblings and the special case of the person who leaves no direct heir. It addresses unlawful sexual relations and the path to repentance, women's rights in marriage and protection from financial abuse, prohibited degrees of marriage, and marriage to bondwomen for those who cannot afford free women. It speaks of Allah's grace and guidance, of avoiding exploitation and injustice, of avoiding major sins, of contentment and divine provision, of the roles of husbands and wives, of worship that joins tawḥīd (the oneness of Allah) with social responsibility, of divine justice and generosity, of the Day of Judgment with its witnesses and accountability, of purification for prayer, and of warning against those who distort scripture and oppose the truth. It declares shirk (associating partners with Allah) the unforgivable sin, exposes self-righteousness, false claims and envy, and describes the final destinations of punishment and reward. It commands justice, trust and obedience to authority, exposes the hypocrisy of those who reject divine judgment, calls for complete submission to the Prophet's ﷺ judgment, and promises the righteous the company of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous. It deals with military preparation, fighting in Allah's cause and liberating the oppressed, with divine destiny and the inescapability of death, with responsible communication and verifying news, with intercession, with the certainty of resurrection, with the opportunism of hypocrites, with caution in identifying the enemy, with the merit of striving in Allah's cause, with emigration from oppression, with prayer concessions during travel and danger, and with just judgment. It closes with repentance and personal accountability, with the value of good speech and private counsel, with the requirement to believe in all prophets, with the history and sins of the Children of Israel and the truth about ʿĪsā (Jesus), with a universal call to believe in the Messenger ﷺ, with the reward of the humble and the punishment of the arrogant, and with the final inheritance ruling for the person who leaves neither parent nor child. Throughout, the surah returns to one theme: that taqwā is the measure of a person, and that the rights of Allah and the rights of people stand or fall together.

### In short

- A Medinan surah of 176 verses, revealed in Al-Madinah, named "The Women" for its many rulings on women, marriage and the family.
- It opens by commanding taqwā and arguing from the single origin of all humanity to the duty of honouring family ties and fearing Allah, who sees everything.
- It contains much of the Qur'an's family and social law: orphans, marriage, divorce, inheritance, women's rights, and the rights of relatives.
- Its virtues include five verses that Ibn Masʿūd preferred to the whole world, and the Prophet's ﷺ use of its first verse in the marriage sermon.
- Its central message is that taqwā is more powerful than law, and that the rights of Allah and the rights of people stand or fall together.

1.text:
"O humanity! Be mindful of your Lord Who created you from a single soul, and from it He created its mate, and through both He spread countless men and women. And be mindful of Allah—in Whose Name you appeal to one another—and ˹honour˺ family ties. Surely Allah is ever Watchful over you." This verse opens Surah An-Nisa and sets its whole tone. It commands all human beings, men and women, those alive then and those to come until the Day of Judgment, to be mindful of their Lord, and it grounds that command in creation: every human being comes from one soul, Adam, and from Adam's mate, Hawwa (Eve), and from the two of them the whole of humanity spread. Because they share one origin, people are brothers and sisters, and no distinction of race, colour, language or caste may be made the measure of worth. The verse then turns the same command inward: people demand their rights from one another in Allah's name, so the one who expects others to fear Allah must fear Him himself, and the closing words warn against cutting family ties. It ends with the reminder that Allah is always watching.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O humanity!"** addresses all human beings without distinction, men and women, those present at the revelation and those to be born until the Day of Judgment.

**"Be mindful of your Lord"** is the command ittaqu, to fear acting against your Lord. "Lord" (Rabb) was chosen from among Allah's names because He is the One who nurtures and sustains, the One whose lordship a person witnesses at every moment. The thought of rising in antagonism against Him is terribly dangerous. The fear of Allah so commanded has its own justification and wisdom.

**"Who created you from a single soul"** means from Adam alone, Eve's soul being included in his. Allah created all human beings from one person, Adam, peace be unto him, in His wisdom and mercy. It was possible to create them in more than one way, but He chose this one way, tying all of them in a strong bond of brotherhood.

**"And from it He created its mate"** refers to Hawwa (Eve), created from Adam's left rib, from his back while he slept. When Adam woke and saw her he was drawn to her and she to him.

**"And through both He spread countless men and women"** means Allah produced many men and women from Adam and Hawwa and scattered them across the world in varied shapes, colours and languages. In the end their gathering and return is to Allah.

**"And be mindful of Allah"** repeats the command, now with the name Allah, and shows that the surah's laws are not given in cold print like the laws of governments but combined with the training of minds and hearts.

**"In Whose Name you appeal to one another"** refers to the way people demand their rights from others by saying "I ask you by Allah." One who expects others to fear Allah must fear Him himself.

**"And honour family ties"** translates al-arham, the plural of rahm, "womb." The womb is where blood relationship comes from, so maintaining that bond is ilat ar-rahm and severing it is qat ar-rahm. The command is not to cut relations with one's kin but to keep and honour them. Ibrahim, Mujahid and Al-Hasan took the mutual-rights phrase in this sense, while Ad-Dahhak said it means fearing Allah when conducting transactions and contracts, and that Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, Mujahid, Al-Hasan, Ad-Dahhak, Ar-Rabi and others took the command to honour the womb as a command not to cut family ties.

**"Surely Allah is ever Watchful over you"** means He watches all your deeds and sees every circumstance, including the intentions and motives of the heart. Doing things half-heartedly, or only for fear of embarrassment, is not accepted. Allah's watchfulness is echoed in "And Allah is Witness over all things" (58:6). The people of Makkah were addressed here, and they used to implore one another by ties of kinship, asking "I ask you by Allah" or "For God's sake."

### Why taqwa opens the surah

The last verse of Surah Al-Imran ended with an exhortation to taqwa, the fear of Allah. Here taqwa appears as a command. The previous surah had spoken of battles, of the treatment of opponents, and of misappropriation of spoils. This surah turns to the rights a person owes to those closest to him: orphans, relatives, wives. Some of these rights can be enforced by law, like buying and selling, lease and wages. Others, the rights of children, parents, husband and wife, and of relatives toward one another, depend on civilised behaviour, respect, love and care, and above all on a genuine desire to do good. Such things cannot be weighed or settled by agreement, so the only way to secure them is taqwa, the fear of Allah and of what comes in the life to come. Taqwa, on this view, is more effective than government and law together. The verse serves as an introduction to the injunctions that follow: it dissuades people from usurping divine rights while, by telling them they are children of the same father, it gives love, mutual sympathy and concern as the working basis of common life, so that the rights of relatives, orphans and married couples may be fulfilled from the heart.

### The bond of brotherhood

All human beings are one by birth and can trace their origin to the same man and woman as father and mother. This unity grows tighter in families, and decent behaviour among kin matters more. Good behaviour between fellow human beings is important not only morally but as a matter of personal concern, because everyone is governed by Allah, who as Reckoner for all will decide the eternal future of everyone in the Hereafter, requiting them according to their actions. A person should not treat his dealings with others as merely human business but as a matter between himself and God. He should fear the grip of God and adhere to the bounds set by God. A report says God proclaimed, "I shall associate Myself with one who strengthens the ties of kinship and detach Myself from one who severs them." This shows that attachment to God is tested through dealings with others: fearing God while honouring others' rights is true veneration, and loving people is loving their Creator. Fair dealing and compassion are general social duties, yet so vital to family life that they rank second only to God. Allah watches over a person and nothing he does escapes Him. Rather, He takes it into account and repays accordingly.

### The hadiths about kinship

Several hadiths develop the command. The Prophet said, "Whoever likes to have his livelihood made plentiful and his age extended for him should maintain good relations with his near of kin." Abdullah ibn Salam reported that when the Prophet came to Madinah al-Tayyibah the first words he heard were: "Make a habit of greeting one another with salam, feeding people for Allah's pleasure, treating near relations well, and praying by night while others sleep, and you will enter Paradise in peace." Maymunah, the Mother of the Faithful, freed a bondwoman and was told that giving her to her maternal uncle would have brought a greater reward, and the Prophet said that charity to the needy is charity while charity to a near relative is twofold: charity and kinship. He also warned: "A breaker of blood relationships shall not enter Paradise," and "Mercy shall not descend upon a people among whom there is a breaker of blood relationships." A hadith about the rib says that woman was created from a rib, and that the most curved part of the rib is its upper part, so trying to straighten it breaks it while leaving it keeps it crooked. Another authentic hadith says, "Worship Allah as if you see Him, for even though you cannot see Him, He sees you."

### The marriage sermon and charity

The word ittaqu, translated here as "fear," means "fear acting against your Lord," and this is perhaps why the Prophet used to recite this verse as part of his address when solemnising a marriage. Reciting it in the khutbah of nikah (the marriage sermon) is a perennial revival of the sunnah (the Prophet's practice). The verse was also recited to a delegation from Mudar who came wearing striped woollen clothes out of poverty: after the Zuhr prayer the Prophet stood and gave a speech in which he recited "O mankind! Have taqwa of your Lord, Who created you from a single person" to the end of the verse, and also "O you who believe! Have taqwa of Allah. And let every person look to what he has sent forth for the tomorrow" (59:18), and encouraged them to give sadaqah (charity), saying, "A man gave sadaqah from his dinar, from his dirham, from his sa of wheat, from his sa of dates." Muslim recorded this, and Ahmad and the collectors of the sunan recorded it from Ibn Masud. Jarir bin Abdullah Al-Bajali reported it.

### The inner meaning of godwariness

The verse calls for making godwariness (taqwa) one's shelter. Godwariness means taking the commands of the shariah as a shield, so that the arrows of prohibition do not reach the servant. It has three levels: first, taking refuge in the sentence of tawhid (the oneness of Allah) and avoiding every associationism. Second, taking refuge in obedience and stepping away from the path of disobedience. Third, taking refuge in caution and fleeing from ambiguity. Whoever climbs these way stations of godwariness truthfully will reach deliverance without fail, for the Qur'an says, "God will deliver those who were godwary" (39:61), and "Whosoever is wary of God, He will appoint a way out for him and He will provide for him from whence he never reckoned" (65:2-3). Whenever someone takes hold of godwariness, God will ease his deliverance from every suffering and send provision from where he has no hope.

The story is told of the sister of Bishr Hafi, who went to see Ahmad Hanbal and asked whether it was permissible to work her spindle on the roof by the light of the Tahirids' torch. Ahmad asked whether she could tolerate such godwariness, and when she said she was the sister of Bishr Hafi he wept and said that godwariness like that was permissible only in the household of Bishr Hafi, and that she should emulate her brother. A report is quoted in which MuṣṬafā, narrating from his Lord, says that when He knows that what dominates over His servant's heart is being occupied with Him, He puts the servant's appetite into supplicating Him and conversing with Him, and that when the servant desires to be negligent of Him, He comes between him and his negligence. "Those are my friends in truth. Those are the champions." He is saying that when the servant wants only Him, knows only Him and belongs only to Him, He turns the face of His heart toward him, shuts the door of all desires and appetites, and gives him ease on the carpet of passion, holding the sword of beginningless jealousy over his head so that he may not look at another. "Today I will entrust him to the policeman of godwariness so that I may keep him under the protection of My shariah." Tomorrow he will rest in the seat of truthfulness (54:55) before At-ness, for "the godwary will be in the midst of gardens and a river, in a seat of truthfulness, at an Omnipotent King" (54:54-55).

The verse also speaks of creation as a pair. The Lord who created everything as a pair made a spouse appear for everyone, joining each with a likeness, for unity and solitariness are an attribute specific to Him. It has been narrated in one of the books, "I have given the things mates so that My unity will be inferred." And from the offspring of one upright individual God brought forth many thousands of creatures with diverse natures and colours, forms and conducts: each has another colour, nature, character, state and aspiration, and no two people are alike in nature and visage. "So glory be to Him whose predetermined things have no end and whose objects of knowledge have no limit!" The watcher is the One who hears hearts without asking, who knows deeds without inquiry, and who never tires in striving. This is an admonishment of the servant: since he knows that God gives ear to hearts and keeps His eyes on deeds and words, he should put watchfulness to work and carry out God's rightful due. Watchfulness means the servant keeps his heart turned toward the Real and the Real's gaze before his eyes. Hence MuṣṬafā said, "When you do not like people seeing something from you, do not do it while you are alone." In this meaning they have sung, "When you are alone with yourself one day, do not say, 'I'm alone.' Say, 'Over me is a Watcher.'"

### The virtues of the surah

Ibn Abbas said, "Ask me about Surah An-Nisa, for I learned the Qur'an when I was still young," and Al-Hakim graded it sahih by the standards of the two Sahihs, though neither collected it. Al-Hakim recorded in his Mustadrak that Ibn Masud said five verses in Surah An-Nisa outweigh the world and all it contains: "Surely, Allah wrongs not even the weight of an atom" (4:40). "If you avoid the great sins which you are forbidden to do" (4:31). "Verily, Allah forgives not that partners should be set up with Him, but He forgives except that to whom He wills" (4:48). "If they, when they had been unjust to themselves, had come to you" (4:64), and "And whoever does evil or wrongs himself, but afterwards seeks Allah's forgiveness, he will find Allah Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful" (4:110). Al-Awfi reported Ibn Abbas as saying the surah was revealed in Al-Madinah, and Ibn Marduwyah recorded like statements from Abdullah bin Az-Zubayr and Zayd bin Thabit. The surah is Madinan.

### In short

- The verse commands all humanity to be mindful of their Lord and grounds the command in creation: all come from Adam and Hawwa, so all are brothers and sisters.
- It warns against cutting family ties and reminds that people who invoke Allah's name in their dealings must fear Him themselves.
- It closes with the reminder that Allah is always watching, which is the reason to fear Him.
- The material adds a long spiritual reading of godwariness, its three levels, and the watchfulness of God over the servant.
- The surah's virtues include five verses preferred by Ibn Masud and Ibn Abbas's claim to know it well.

2.text:
"Give orphans their wealth when they reach maturity, and do not exchange your worthless possessions for their valuables, nor cheat them by mixing their wealth with your own. For this would indeed be a great sin." This verse commands the guardian of an orphan to hand over the orphan's property in full once the orphan has grown up and can manage it, and it forbids two ways of cheating: swapping the orphan's good property for the guardian's bad property, and mixing the orphan's wealth with the guardian's so that it gets eaten up. It ends by calling such conduct a great sin. The verse is the first of several in this surah that protect orphans, and it connects to the surah's opening command of taqwa, because the rights of orphans are rights of kinship that cannot be enforced by courts alone.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Give orphans their wealth"** means hand over what belongs to them when they reach maturity and sound judgement. An orphan (yatim) is a child whose father has died. In the terminology of Islamic law, a yatim is a child whose father has died. The word literally means "the lone one," and a lone pearl in its shell is called an orphan pearl (Ad-Durr al-Yatim). Orphanhood ends at puberty. The property may have come by gift or inheritance, and its protection and upkeep fall on the guardian, whether appointed by the father or by the government. The guardian must spend on the orphan's maintenance from the orphan's own funds, but should not hand the property over before maturity, since an immature child may lose it, which is haram. So "give" here first means protect and conserve, so that the property can be handed over intact at the right time. A detailed explanation of mixing property appears in connection with 2:220, Section 27 of Surah al-Baqarah.

**"When they reach maturity"** marks the time when the orphan is no longer a minor and can distinguish what is good for him from what is not, as clarified later in this surah.

**"And do not exchange your worthless possessions for their valuables"** forbids substituting bad for good: a lean goat for a healthy one, a bad coin for a good one. Some guardians let the number of items stay the same while swapping a good item of the orphan's for a bad item of their own, excusing themselves by saying "a sheep for a sheep" or "a dirham for a dirham." Such substitution is a breach of trust even when the count is unchanged, and it also covers any deal that ends in loss for the orphan.

**"Nor cheat them by mixing their wealth with your own"** forbids pooling the orphan's property with the guardian's and consuming from the common fund, whether the holdings are kept together or separately. Even a religiously careful person may fall into this, so the verse warns against it. The word "eat" is used because eating is a major use of property, but in usage "eating up" covers every kind of unlawful consumption.

**"For this would indeed be a great sin"** is the warning. Sayyidna Ibn Abbas said "hub" (great sin) is an Ethiopian word used in Arabic for a major sin. Any unlawful appropriation of an orphan's property, whether by lack of supervision, substitution, or mixing, is a great sin. A stern warning to those who eat up an orphan's property appears toward the end of this section at 4:10.

### Protecting orphans as a test of taqwa

Orphan boys and girls are the weakest members of a family and society, so dealing with them justly is a severe test of being imbued with the fear of Allah. Orphans deserve just and compassionate treatment with maximum protection of their rights, as they say. It is a major sin to divide joint property so that some receive valuable shares and others worthless shares, merely to make the lists tally. One reading adds that whoever is given charge over others and acts unjustly toward them has the Lord as his adversary, who avenges His servants what He will not avenge for His own sake, while the protector who acts with justice and beneficence has his right protected by God. Muqatil and al-Kalbi said the verse was revealed about a man from Ghatafan who had a great fortune belonging to his orphaned nephew. When the verse was revealed he separated the nephew's wealth from his own for fear of sin. A report tells that the nephew claimed the fortune at puberty, the uncle refused, and they took the dispute to the Prophet, who then received this verse. The uncle surrendered the wealth and the Prophet said that whoever is saved from the stinginess of his ego in this way will abide in Allah's Garden. When the youth spent the wealth in Allah's way, the Prophet said the reward is confirmed but the sin still persists, and when asked how, he said the reward is for the youth while the sin persists for his father.

### The prohibition of marrying female orphans without a dowry

The next part of the verse (and the following verses) addresses marriage. If a guardian fears he cannot deal justly with an orphan girl in his care, he should marry other women of his choice, two or three or four. If he fears he cannot do justice even then, one only, or what his right hand possesses. This was revealed about a man who was caring for a female orphan, married her without desiring to, mixing her money with his and keeping her portion from her. Aishah explained that the verse concerns the orphan girl who lives with her guardian and shares his property: her wealth and beauty may tempt him to marry her without an adequate dowry that another suitor might have given, so guardians were forbidden to marry such orphan girls unless they treated them justly and gave a suitable dowry. Otherwise they were to marry other women. When people asked the Prophet again, Allah revealed 4:127, where "those whom you desire to marry" refers to the guardian who does not desire to marry an orphan girl under his supervision because she is neither wealthy nor beautiful. Guardians were forbidden to marry orphan girls who had property and beauty unless they were just to them, since they usually avoid marrying girls who are neither beautiful nor wealthy.

### The permission to marry four women

**"Two or three or four"** means a man may marry as many women as he likes other than orphan girls, up to four. Allah's statement in 35:1 about angels with wings, two or three or four, does not mean other angels do not have more than four wings, since some angels have more. But men are prohibited from marrying more than four wives, because the verse specifies what men are allowed. If more were allowed, the verse would have mentioned it, as Ibn Abbas and the majority of scholars stated. Ahmad recorded that Salim reported from his father that Ghilan bin Salamah Ath-Thaqafi had ten wives when he became Muslim, and the Prophet told him, "Choose any four of them and divorce the rest." During the reign of Umar, Ghilan divorced his remaining wives and divided his money among his children. Umar rebuked him, saying the devil had conveyed news of his imminent death, and ordered him to take back his wives and money or else his grave would be stoned like the grave of Abu Righal of Thamud, who was saved while in the Sacred Area but tormented when he left it. Ash-Shafii, At-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ad-Daraqutni and Al-Bayhaqi collected the hadith up to the Prophet's statement "Choose any four of them". Only Ahmad collected the full version. The Prophet's command to keep only four, even for a man who already had more upon embracing Islam, shows that no one may keep more than four wives at any time, and this applies even more to marrying more than four.

### Marrying only one wife

If a man fears he cannot do justice between his wives by marrying more than one, he should marry only one, or satisfy himself with female captives, for treating captives equally is not obligatory but recommended. In another verse Allah says, "You will never be able to do perfect justice between wives even if it is your ardent desire" (4:129). "That is nearer to prevent you from ta'ulu" means from doing injustice. Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Marduwyah and Abu Hatim Ibn Hibban recorded in his Sahih that Aishah said the Prophet said this verse means from doing injustice. But Ibn Abi Hatim said his father held this hadith to be mistakenly attributed to the Prophet and that it should be attributed to Aishah. Ibn Abi Hatim lists Ibn Abbas, Aishah, Mujahid, Ikrimah, Al-Hasan, Abu Malik, Abu Razin, An-Nakhai, Ash-Shabi, Ad-Dahhak, Ata Al-Khurasani, Qatadah, As-Suddi and Muqatil bin Hayyan as saying ta'ulu means to deviate from justice.

### The dowry is obligatory

**"And give to the women whom you marry their saduqat (dowry) as a nihlah (gift)."** Ali bin Abi Talhah reported Ibn Abbas saying nihlah refers to the dowry. Muhammad bin Ishaq narrated from Az-Zuhri that Urwah said Aishah said nihlah means obligatory. Muqatil, Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj said it means obligatory, and Ibn Jurayj added "specified". Ibn Zayd said in Arabic nihlah refers to what is necessary. So Allah commands that a man not marry unless he gives his wife her right, and no one after the Prophet may marry a woman except with the required dowry, nor by false promises about it. The man must pay the dowry with a good heart, as he gives a gift with a good heart. If the wife, of her own good pleasure, remits part or all of it, her husband may take it and enjoy it without fear of harm.

### In short

- The verse commands guardians to protect orphans' property and hand it over at maturity, and forbids swapping bad for good or mixing it with their own.
- Such conduct is a great sin, and protecting orphans is a severe test of taqwa.
- The verse also regulates marriage: a guardian who fears injustice to an orphan girl should marry other women, up to four, or only one.
- The dowry is obligatory, and a wife may freely remit part or all of it.
- The material adds the stories of the Ghatafan orphan and Ghilan bin Salamah, and the rulings drawn from them.

3.text:
"If you fear you might fail to give orphan women their due rights if you were to marry them, then marry other women of your choice—two, three, or four. But if you are afraid you will fail to maintain justice, then content yourselves with one or those bondwomen in your possession. This way you are less likely to commit injustice." This verse continues the protection of orphans by addressing a specific abuse: a guardian marrying an orphan girl under his care in order to keep her property, fixing a low dowry and treating her as he pleases. It commands that if he fears he cannot do justice to such a girl, he should marry other women instead, up to four, and if he fears he cannot maintain justice even then, only one, or a bondwoman. The verse thus restricts polygamy and makes justice the condition for it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If you fear you might fail to give orphan women their due rights"** refers to the guardian who holds an orphan girl and fears he cannot treat her justly in marriage, especially when her wealth and beauty tempt him to marry her without an adequate dowry.

**"Then marry other women of your choice—two, three, or four"** permits marrying other women instead, up to four, as many as he likes, provided they are lawful for him. The expression "ma taba" means women lawful for him, and also those he desires. There is no contradiction, since it means women he desires who are also lawful in the shariah.

**"But if you are afraid you will fail to maintain justice"** addresses the fear of not being able to do justice between wives.

**"Then content yourselves with one"** commands marrying only one wife when justice between several cannot be maintained.

**"Or those bondwomen in your possession"** permits satisfying oneself with a bondwoman, for treating bondwomen equally is not obligatory but recommended.

**"This way you are less likely to commit injustice"** means this is nearer to preventing deviation from justice (ta'ulu), which scholars explained as deviating from justice.

### The abuse addressed

During the time of ignorance, guardians of orphan girls would pick those with good looks or valuable property, marry them or arrange their marriage to their sons, fix the lowest possible dowry, and maintain them as they pleased, since their fathers were not there to protect their rights. A narration in Sahih al-Bukhari from Aishah reports that a man had an orphan girl under his guardianship and a fruit farm in which she held a share. He married her and, instead of giving her a dowry from his own pocket, took her share in the farm. Thereupon this verse was revealed: if you fear you cannot do justice to the orphans, marry the women you like. The verse therefore lays down total vigilance so that the marital rights of orphan girls are not violated. The responsibility is placed on people themselves to fear Allah and do what is right, and also on the enforcing agencies of government to oversee that no such violation occurs.

### Marriage of minors

The word yatama here means orphan girls. In the terminology of the shariah, a yatim is a boy or girl who has not yet attained puberty, so the verse proves that a guardian may give an orphan girl in marriage while she is a minor, provided the decision is based on wisdom and her future welfare. Orphan girls who have attained puberty are entitled to choose their husbands freely on the basis of their majority, but in practice girls tend to be modest and shy and may accept what their guardians do in good faith, so guardians must stay clear of violating their rights.

### Polygamy before Islam

Having more than one wife was considered permissible in all religions before Islam. The custom prevailed in Arabia, India, Iran, Egypt, Babylon and elsewhere. The Europeans later made multiplicity of marriage impermissible, which resulted in multiplicity of concubines and girl-friends out of wedlock. Vedic teachings permit unlimited wives, and Shri Krishna had hundreds of wives. Davenport, a Christian writer, deduced from the Bible that plurality of wives is favourable and a source of blessing. Father Nixon, John Milton and Isac Taylor supported this view. The truth is that a religion or law aiming to establish an infrastructure against adultery serves as a remedial approach to the problem of a comparatively larger female population. Nations that do not permit plurality of wives must live with rampant adultery. During the early period of Islam the custom continued without limit, and people took too many wives to satisfy greed, then could not do justice, so their wives lived like prisoners. The Qur'an stopped this injustice by restricting plurality to four and warning that equality in fulfilling the rights of wives taken at the same time must be maintained faithfully. The expression "ma taba" was explained by Hasan al-Basri, Ibn Jubair and Ibn Malik as "ma halla," women lawful for you. Others took the literal meaning "whom you like". There is no contradiction, since it means women you like who are also lawful in the shariah.

### The restriction to four

The Qur'an restricted multiplicity of wives by declaring that keeping more than four women in marriage is forbidden (haram), and gave stern warning against contravening this. The Prophet made this clearer: Ghailan ibn Aslamah al-Thaqafi embraced Islam with ten wives, and the Prophet told him to select and retain four and divorce the rest. Ghailan obeyed. Later, during the caliphate of Umar, Ghailan divorced the four and distributed his assets among his sons. Umar summoned him and said he had done this to deprive the women of inheritance, which was gross injustice, and ordered him to revoke the divorce and take back his assets, or else he would take possession of all and order his grave stoned like the grave of Abu Righal of Thamud, who was saved while in the Sacred Area but tormented when he left it. Ash-Shafii, At-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ad-Daraqutni and Al-Bayhaqi collected the hadith up to the Prophet's statement "Choose any four of them". Only Ahmad collected the full version. Had it been allowed to keep more than four, the Prophet would have allowed Ghilan to keep more, since they all embraced Islam with him. His command to keep only four shows no one may keep more than four under any circumstances.

### Only one wife where injustice is likely

After allowing up to four, the verse says if you fear you will not maintain equity, keep to one woman, or a bondwoman you own. Having more than one wife is permissible only on condition that equality is maintained as required by the shariah and the rights of all are fulfilled. If one lacks this capability, the rule is to keep to one wife. The Qur'anic expression for bondwoman has special conditions that generally do not exist today, so starting to live with someone out of wedlock by calling her a bondwoman is non sequitur and patently haram. Marriages within the limit of four are valid, but any shortcoming in treating wives equally is a grave sin, challengeable in an Islamic court. The Prophet laid great emphasis on maintaining full equality and justice between wives and demonstrated it in his own conduct. A hadith says anyone who has two wives and cannot fulfil their rights equally will be raised on the Day of Doom with one shoulder drooping. Equality is necessary in things within man's control, such as personal expenses and overnight stays. As for the natural inclination of the heart, there is no accountability, provided it does not affect matters within control. The Prophet treated his wives with full equality in everything within his control, yet prayed, "O Allah, this is my equalization in what I control, so do not hold me accountable in matters You control and I do not." Another verse says, "You shall be unable to maintain perfect equality between the women" (4:129), referring to love and the tilt of the heart, which are beyond man's power. Yet total indifference to the other wife is not permissible. The justice mentioned in "if you fear you will not maintain equity, keep to one woman" refers to justice in matters of choice and volition, any discrepancy in which is a great sin.

5.text:
"Do not entrust the incapable among your dependants with your wealth which Allah has made a means of support for you—but feed and clothe them from it, and speak to them kindly." This verse commands that property not be handed over to those who cannot manage it, whether children, women, or the feeble-minded, since Allah has made wealth a means of support for people. Instead, the guardian should feed and clothe them from it and speak to them kindly. It protects both the property and the dependants.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do not entrust the incapable among your dependants with your wealth"** forbids giving property to those who do not know how to manage it well, including children, women, and the feeble-minded, as Ad-Dahhak reported Ibn Abbas saying, and as Ibn Masud, Al-Hakam bin Uyaynah, Al-Hasan and Ad-Dahhak also said: "Women and boys." Sa'id bin Jubayr said "the unwise" refers to orphans. Mujahid, Ikrimah and Qatadah said they are women. The same tafsir was reported from Abu Musa al-Ashari, and al-Tabari adopted it. The generality of the words includes all children, orphans and non-orphans.

**"Which Allah has made a means of support for you"** means wealth is a means of livelihood and support, not for luxury or pride.

**"But feed and clothe them from it"** commands the guardian to spend on their food and clothing from the property.

**"And speak to them kindly"** commands kind words, keeping good relations, and making a firm commitment to give them their property when they gain sound judgement.

### Holding property in escrow

The verse affirms the role of property in man's economic effort and corrects the general weakness in protecting it. People sometimes hand over property to inexperienced minor children and ill-informed women out of natural love, which results in waste and quick poverty. Ibn Abbas explained that one should not hand over all one's property to feeble-minded children and women and become dependent on them. Rather, hold the property in safe custody, spend on them as necessary, and if they demand possession, explain honestly and reasonably, saying that it is there for them when they grow up. The property of orphans remains under the guardian's safe custody as if it were his own, until they become mature and discerning, as verse 2 commands giving orphans their property. Ali bin Abi Talhah reported Ibn Abbas saying one should not give one's wealth, which Allah has made a means of sustenance, to wife or children, but hold on to it, take care of it, and be the one who spends on them. Mujahid said "speak to them words of kindness and justice" refers to kindness and keeping good relations. The verse commands kind treatment in deed with family and those under one's care.

### The value of property

Protecting property is necessary and wasting it is a sin. A person killed while defending his property is a shahid (martyr), similar to being killed in defence of one's life. The Prophet said, "Whosoever is killed while protecting his property is counted among Muslim martyrs." He also said, "For a good man, his good and clean property is the best asset of his life," and "Being rich is not harmful for one who fears Allah." The anti-wealth teachings of many saints apply only to those who spend lustily-earned wealth for sinful purposes. Poverty can take one to the point of being a disbeliever. Sufyan al-Thawri said that previously owning wealth was not considered good, but today wealth is a shield of the true Muslim, and whoever has wealth should make it serve him well, since these are times when one may first spend his faith to take care of a need. The verse also connects to 4:10, the stern warning to those who eat up an orphan's property. One reading takes "the foolish" as those who keep you from the Real and distract you from the Lord, those dependents and children who prefer their worldly portions over the rights of God. It is better to be generous than withholding for the liberation of the heart, and when your lower self calls you to spend in a useless way you are the most foolish of the foolish, so do not give in.

6.text:
"Test the competence of the orphans until they reach a marriageable age. Then if you feel they are capable of sound judgment, return their wealth to them. And do not consume it wastefully and hastily before they grow up to demand it. If the guardian is well-off, they should not take compensation. But if the guardian is poor, let them take a reasonable provision. When you give orphans back their property, call in witnesses. And sufficient is Allah as a vigilant Reckoner." This verse commands testing orphans before they reach maturity, handing over their property once they show sound judgement, and not consuming it wastefully or hastily. It permits a poor guardian to take a reasonable provision and requires witnesses when returning the property. It ends with the reminder that Allah is sufficient as Reckoner.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Test the competence of the orphans"** means test their intelligence through small assignments of buying and selling before they become pubert and marriageable, to determine their ability to conduct transactions on their own. Imam Abu Hanifah deduced from this that transactions entered into by minor children with the permission of their guardian are sound, valid and operative.

**"Until they reach a marriageable age"** means until they become pubert and mature, which is the time of special assessment.

**"Then if you feel they are capable of sound judgment"** means once it is clear they understand profit and loss and handle their affairs satisfactorily.

**"Return their wealth to them"** commands handing over the property in full.

**"And do not consume it wastefully and hastily before they grow up to demand it"** forbids using up the wealth overstepping the limits Allah approved, or rushing to consume it for fear they will take it when they reach maturity.

**"If the guardian is well-off, they should not take compensation"** means a rich guardian should abstain from the orphan's property.

**"But if the guardian is poor, let them take a reasonable provision"** permits a poor guardian to take in proportion to his work, or as a loan to be paid back, in measure such that he is not in need of the orphan's wealth.

**"When you give orphans back their property, call in witnesses"** requires witnessing the transaction to protect rights and prevent disputes.

**"And sufficient is Allah as a vigilant Reckoner"** reminds that Allah suffices as witness and takes account of all.

### Testing and maturity

The verse divides children into three stages: minority before puberty, after puberty, and after self-reliance and discretion in conducting personal affairs (rushd as opposed to safahah). During the first stage, guardians should educate and train them through hands-on experience. Once they become mature, pubert and marriageable, the guardian should check their state of growth in terms of experience, intelligence and dealings, and once dependable, hand over the property. Real maturity is not tied to a particular count of years but depends on particular indicators and signs experienced by adults entering the threshold of adulthood. The verse was revealed about Thabit ibn Rifa'ah al-Ansari. The age of marrying according to al-Shafi'i is the completion of fifteen years. Test them when near maturity by giving them part of their wealth to see how they manage it. Perceiving maturity means decency and integrity, generosity and preservation of honour, keeping company with elders and striving to look to the good and perform acts of devotion. The one who is mature (rashid) is the one who is guided to his Lord and does not rely on his own power or strength when a need arises.

### The poor guardian's provision

A poor guardian may take a reasonable provision from the orphan's property in proportion to his work, or as a loan to be paid back. The condition is "in proportion to need." Many fix an insignificant monthly emolument on paper to satisfy legal requirements but spend recklessly beyond it. The last words "Allah is sufficient for reckoning" invite everyone to realize that the man who stays untouched by unlawful acquisitions is the one who fears the final accounting by Allah, and the ability to do so comes from Allah. Property is a means of livelihood, not for luxury or pride. Misappropriation of anyone's belongings is akin to creating a breach in God's arrangement of bestowing livelihood upon His servants. In the case of an orphan, the weakest member of society, it is even more imperative that his property be well-protected and he be dealt with in fairness and justice. A justified settlement with orphans should be recorded in writing and witnessed so that the executor's responsibility is honourably discharged with no question of future disputes. Whenever one takes someone's affairs in hand, he must proceed with the realization that any injustice is in the knowledge of God, who will catch hold of the arbiter on the Day of Reckoning and punish him severely. 11.text:
"Allah commands you regarding your children: the share of the male will be twice that of the female. If you leave only two or more females, their share is two-thirds of the estate. But if there is only one female, her share will be one-half. Each parent is entitled to one-sixth if you leave offspring. But if you are childless and your parents are the only heirs, then your mother will receive one-third. But if you leave siblings, then your mother will receive one-sixth—after the fulfilment of bequests and debts. Be fair to your parents and children, as you do not fully know who is more beneficial to you. This is an obligation from Allah. Surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise." This verse sets out the rules of inheritance: the male receives twice the share of the female. Two or more daughters receive two-thirds. One daughter receives one-half. Each parent receives one-sixth if there are children. If childless, the mother receives one-third. If there are siblings, the mother receives one-sixth. All this is after bequests and debts. It ends by saying these fixed shares are an obligation from Allah, who is All-Knowing, All-Wise.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah commands you regarding your children"** introduces the inheritance rules for children.

**"The share of the male will be twice that of the female"** means the male gets a portion equal to that of two females.

**"If you leave only two or more females, their share is two-thirds of the estate"** gives two-thirds to two or more daughters.

**"But if there is only one female, her share will be one-half"** gives one-half to a single daughter.

**"Each parent is entitled to one-sixth if you leave offspring"** gives each parent one-sixth when there are children.

**"But if you are childless and your parents are the only heirs, then your mother will receive one-third"** gives the mother one-third when there are no children.

**"But if you leave siblings, then your mother will receive one-sixth"** reduces the mother's share to one-sixth when siblings exist.

**"After the fulfilment of bequests and debts"** means bequests and debts are paid first.

**"Be fair to your parents and children, as you do not fully know who is more beneficial to you"** reminds that one does not know which relative is more beneficial.

**"This is an obligation from Allah"** declares these fixed shares are ordained by Allah.

**"Surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise"** affirms Allah's knowledge and wisdom.

### The reason for revealing the verse

Al-Bukhari recorded that Jabir bin Abdullah said the Prophet came visiting him on foot with Abu Bakr at Banu Salamah's dwellings and found him unconscious. He performed ablution and poured water on him, and Jabir regained consciousness and asked what to do with his money. This verse was later revealed. Muslim and An-Nasa'i also recorded it, and the remainder of the six compilers collected it. Ahmad recorded from Jabir that the wife of Sa'd bin Ar-Rabi' came to the Prophet and said her husband was killed as a martyr at Uhud and his uncle took their money and left nothing for his two daughters, who would not be married without money. The Prophet said Allah will decide, and later the verse was revealed and the Prophet sent word to the uncle commanding him to give two-thirds to Sa'd's two daughters and one-eighth to their mother, and whatever is left is his. Abu Dawud, At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah collected this hadith. The first hadith from Jabir was about the case of the last verse in the surah (4:176), for at that time Jabir had sisters and did not have daughters, parents or offspring to inherit from him. Yet it was mentioned here as Al-Bukhari did.

### Learning the shares

This verse, the following, and the last verse in this surah contain the knowledge of Al-Fara'id (inheritance). The knowledge of Al-Fara'id is derived from these three verses and from the hadiths on this subject which explain them. Learning this knowledge is encouraged, especially the specific things mentioned in the verses. Ibn Uyaynah said knowledge of Al-Fara'id was called half of knowledge, because it affects all people. The verse was commented on by Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Uyaynah, Qatadah, Ar-Rabi, Jabir, Abu Bakr, Sa'd, and others. The verse cites 35:32 and 4:176. Collectors include Abu Dawud, Al-Bukhari, An-Nasa'i, At-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah. Al-Hasan graded the relevant hadith. The verse involves fard, qiyas, salaf, sunnah, shariah, say, hadith, uhud, lot, al-Nuqsan, ʿaṣaba, and related terms. The scholars and terms mentioned include IbnAbHatim and 4176. ### In short

- The male receives twice the female's share.
- Bequests and debts are paid first.

And if a man or a woman leaves neither parents nor children but only a brother or a sister from their mother's side, they will each inherit one-sixth, but if they are more than one, they all will share one-third of the estate—after the fulfilment of bequests and debts without harm to the heirs. This is a commandment from Allah. And Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing." This verse sets out the inheritance shares of spouses and of siblings from the mother's side (kalalah), after bequests and debts, and declares them a commandment from Allah.

### Phrase by phrase

**"You will inherit half of what your wives leave if they are childless"** gives the husband half when the wife leaves no child.

**"But if they have children, then your share is one-fourth"** gives the husband one-fourth when there are children.

**"And your wives will inherit one-fourth of what you leave if you are childless"** gives the wife one-fourth when the husband leaves no child.

**"But if you have children, then your wives will receive one-eighth"** gives the wife one-eighth when there are children.

**"And if a man or a woman leaves neither parents nor children but only a brother or a sister from their mother's side"** introduces the kalalah case.

**"They will each inherit one-sixth"** gives one-sixth to a single sibling from the mother's side.

**"But if they are more than one, they all will share one-third"** gives one-third to multiple siblings from the mother's side.

**"After the fulfilment of bequests and debts"** means debts and bequests are paid first.

**"This is a commandment from Allah"** declares these shares ordained by Allah.

**"And Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing"** affirms Allah's knowledge and forbearance.

### Spousal shares and kalalah

The husband gets half of what his wife leaves if she has no child, and one-fourth if she has a child. The wife gets one-fourth of what her husband leaves if he has no child, and one-eighth if he has a child. Payment of debts comes before fulfilling the will, then the will, then inheritance, and there is consensus on this among scholars. The rule applies to grandchildren as well. If there is more than one wife, they all share the fourth or eighth. Kalalah means the man or woman whose inheritance is in question leaves neither ascendants nor descendants, but has a brother or sister from the mother's side. Each gets one-sixth, and if more than two, they share one-third. The verse cites 30:21. At the beginning of Islam, if a woman committed adultery as stipulated by sufficient proof, she was confined to her home without leave until she died. This verse states that Allah accepts the repentance of those who do evil in ignorance and foolishness and repent soon afterwards, and He will pardon them. ### Phrase by phrase

### Repentance accepted until death

Every person who disobeys Allah, even willfully, is ignorant while committing the act of disobedience. Mujahid and others said every person who disobeys Allah by mistake or intentionally is ignorant until he refrains from the sin. Qatadah said the Companions used to say every sin the servant commits, he commits out of ignorance. Abdur-Razzaq narrated that Ma'mar said Qatadah said the Companions agreed that every sin committed by intention or otherwise is committed in ignorance. Ibn Jurayj said a narrator narrated that Mujahid said every person who disobeys Allah is ignorant while committing the act. Ata bin Abi Rabah said something similar. Abu Salih said Ibn Abbas commented it is because of one's ignorance that he commits the error. Ali bin Abi Talhah reported Ibn Abbas saying "and repent soon afterwards" means until just before he looks at the angel of death. Ad-Dahhak said everything before death is "soon afterwards." Al-Hasan Al-Basri said it means just before his last breath leaves his throat. Ikrimah said all of this life is "soon afterwards." Imam Ahmad recorded that Ibn Umar said the Messenger said, "Allah accepts the repentance of the servant as long as the soul does not reach the throat." At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah also collected it. At-Tirmidhi said "Hasan Gharib." By mistake Ibn Majah mentioned Abdullah bin Amr as narrator, but the correct narrator is Abdullah bin Umar bin Al-Khattab. The verse cites 6:158, 40:84 and 66:8. It was commented on by Mujahid, Qatadah, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Abbas, Ad-Dahhak, Al-Hasan Al-Basri, Ikrimah, Ali bin Abi Talhah, Abu Salih, and others. Collectors include At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah. The verse involves tawbah, shirk, ummah, adam, musa, aaron, yusuf, pharaoh, salah, zakah, and related terms. This verse forbids approaching prayer while intoxicated until one knows what one is saying, and while sexually impure except when passing through, until bathing. It permits tayammum with clean earth when water is unavailable due to illness, travel, or other causes. And affirms Allah is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving.

**"O believers! Do not approach prayer while intoxicated"** forbids approaching prayer while drunk.

**"Until you are aware of what you say"** means until one knows what one is saying.

**"Nor in a state of full impurity"** forbids attending while sexually impure.

**"Unless you merely pass through the mosque"** permits passing through.

**"But if you are ill, on a journey, or have relieved yourselves, or been intimate with your wives and cannot find water"** lists excuses.

**"Then purify yourselves with clean earth"** commands tayammum.

**"Wiping your faces and hands"** describes the wiping.

**"And Allah is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving"** affirms Allah's pardon and forgiveness.

### Intoxication and purity

Prayer while drunk is forbidden, for one does not know the meaning of what he is saying in that state, and attending the Masjids while sexually impure is forbidden, except when one is merely passing through the Masjid from one door to another. This Ayah was revealed before alcohol consumption was completely prohibited. In that Hadith, the Messenger of Allah recited this Ayah to Umar, who said, "O Allah! Explain the ruling about Khamr (intoxicants) for us in a plain manner." When this Ayah was revealed, the Prophet recited it to Umar, who still said, "O Allah! Explain the ruling about Khamr (intoxicants) for us in a plain manner." After that, they would not drink alcohol close to the time of prayer. When Allah's statement, "O you who believe! alcoholic drinks, gambling, Al-Ansab, and Al-Azlam are an abomination of Shayatan's handiwork. So avoid that in order that you may be successful" (5:90), until, "So, will you not then abstain" (5:91) was revealed, Umar said, "We abstain, we abstain." In another narration, when the Ayah in Surat An-Nisa' was revealed, "O you who believe! Do not approach Salah while you are in a druken state until you know what you are saying," at the time of prayer, the Messenger of Allah would have someone proclaim. "Let not any drunk approach the prayer." This is the wording collected by Abu Dawud. Sa'd said that four Ayat were revealed concerning him. A man from the Ansar once made some food and invited some Muhajirin and Ansar men to it, and they ate and drank until they became intoxicated. They then boasted about their status. Afterwards a man held a camel's bone and injured Sa'd's nose, leaving a scar ever since. This occurred before Al-Khamr was prohibited, and Allah later revealed, "O you who believe! Approach not AsSalat (the prayer) when you are in a drunken state." Muslim recorded this Hadith, and the collectors of the Sunan recorded it, with the exception of Ibn Majah. Ali bin Abi Talib said that Abdur-Rahman bin Awf made some food to which he invited them and served some alcohol to drink. When they became intoxicated, and the time for prayer came, they asked someone to lead them in prayer. He recited 'Say, O disbelievers! I do not worship that which you worship, but we worship that which you worship.' Allah then revealed something. The verse cites 2:219, 2:237, 5:90, 5:91, 33:49, 33:72, 39:53. It was commented on by Ibn Abbas, A'ishah, Abu Hurayrah, and others. Collectors include Abu Dawud, Al-Bukhari, An-Nasa'i, At-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Majah. The verse involves ghusl, salah, say, shariah, taqwa, tayammum, wudu, and related terms. Allah commands that the trusts be returned to their rightful owners. Al-Hasan narrated that Samurah said that the Messenger of Allah said, "Return the trust to those who entrusted you, and do not betray those who betrayed you." This Hadith was recorded by Imam Ahmad and the collectors of Sunan. This command covers every matter which one is expected to look after, such as Allah's rights on His servants: praying, Zakah, fasting, penalties for sins, vows and so forth. It also includes the rights of the servants toward one another, such as what they entrust each other with, including cases that are not recorded or documented. Allah commands that all types of trusts be fulfilled. Those who do not implement this command in this life will have it extracted from them on the Day of Resurrection. It is recorded in the Sahih that the Messenger of Allah said, "The rights will be rendered back to those to whom they are due, and even the sheep that does not have horns will take revenge from the horned sheep." Ibn Jarir recorded that Ibn Jurayj said about this Ayah that it was revealed concerning 'Uthman bin Talhah. The Messenger of Allah took the key of the Ka'bah from him and entered it on the Day of the victory of Makkah. When the Prophet went out, he was reciting this Ayah. He then called 'Uthman and gave the key back to him. Ibn Jarir also narrated that 'Umar bin Al-Khattab said, "When the Messenger of Allah went out of the Ka'bah, he was reciting this Ayah." ### In short

- A disaster will befall them because of their deeds.
- They will swear they meant goodwill.
- The verse follows the previous ones.

63.text:

This verse states that Allah knows what is in the hearts of the hypocrites. The Prophet should turn aside from them, admonish them, and speak to them a word that reaches their inner selves.

### Phrase by phrase

**"So turn away from them"** commands turning aside from them.

**"Caution them"** commands admonishing them.

**"And give them advice that will shake their very souls"** commands speaking an effective word to reach their inner selves.
